newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania doesn't need currency board-central banker.
newsitem.headline: Romania doesn't need currency board-central banker.

text.p: Romania does not need a tight currency regime, the currency board, proposed by the International Monetary Fund as the last-resort economic remedy to the neighbouring Bulgaria, a senior official said on Friday.
Asked to comment on the International Monetary Fund's recent proposal to bring in the currency board system in Bulgaria, BNR chief economist Daniel Daianu said:
"I'm not for a currency board. We are not in Bulgaria's disastrous situation. This is not a solution for us. A currency board is a belt which can only stiffle the economy."

Under the system, the local currency is anchored at a fixed rate to a hard currency and monetary expansion is controlled by limiting money in circulation to an equivalent of hard currency reserves held by a country.

The IMF has asked Bulgaria to adopt the currency board to stabilise its currency and curb inflation. But the system would force the authorities to give up their power to influence exchange ands interest rates.
"That would mean giving up some instruments of (monetary) policy. Could Romania afford that now? I think it is out of the question," Daianu said.
IMF resident officials in Bucharest were not available for comment and no official body so far suggested Romania should swich to the currency board to answer its own economic problems.

Under a 1994 IMF loan accord Romania set up a free-floating system for the leu currency. But a decison earlier this year to limit the local foreign exchange market to only four market-making dealer banks almost killed trading.
The Fund suspended loan tranches for Romania earlier this year, over forex market curbs followed by slippage in monetary and fiscal policies in an electoral year.
Inflation has recently rebounded reaching an year-on-year 45 percent in September, with Romania plagued by bulging budget and trade deficits.
